李東熈
同考試官訓導郭，批〔揭書出題，本平易，要寫出聖人氣象自難。此作獨能發之，若親炙聖人者，取冠本房無忝。〕
同考試官學正李，批〔形容聖人，千載宛然在目，佳作也。〕
考試官教授李，批〔分明畫出一箇聖人，蓋必用心於學聖之工夫者，欽杖起敬。〕
考試官教授濮，批〔發揮盛德，自中乎禮，理明詞正，僅見此篇。〕
門人記聖人隨其所處之地而言貌有不同焉。蓋鄉黨廟朝，地不同也，則其言貌夫豈同哉？聖人德盛，而周旋中禮，有如是夫！昔門人以孔子之動靜無非至教，故於其言貌無不謹書，蓋曰：
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

“Among the people of his home community, Confucius was gentle and unassuming, as though unable to speak. In the ancestral temple and at court, he spoke fluently, yet with care.”

Li Dongxi

Comment by Associate Examiner Guo, Assistant Instructor: 〔Selecting a passage from the book as a topic is straightforward enough; conveying the sage’s bearing is inherently difficult. This composition alone brings it out, as though its author had personally received the sage’s instruction. It fully deserves first place among the papers in this examining group.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: 〔It portrays the sage so vividly that, a thousand years later, he seems to stand before our eyes. An excellent composition.〕

Comment by Examiner Li, Instructor: 〔It distinctly depicts a sage. Its author must surely have devoted himself to the work of learning to become a sage. It inspires admiration [?] and reverence.〕

Comment by Examiner Pu, Instructor: 〔It expounds the sage’s abundant virtue and his spontaneous conformity to ritual propriety. Its reasoning is clear and its language correct; this essay alone achieves this.〕

The disciples recorded how the sage’s speech and demeanor differed according to where he was. His home community, the ancestral temple, and the court were different settings: how, then, could his speech and demeanor have been the same? Such was the sage’s abundant virtue that his every movement accorded with ritual propriety!

In former times, the disciples considered that everything Confucius did, whether in action or at rest, offered the highest instruction. Thus they carefully recorded every aspect of his speech and demeanor. In effect, they said: …

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
鄉黨者父兄之所居宗族之所聚夫子於此也
何如爾恭欽容而恂恂乎信實之形敦本尚質
而恂恂乎誠慤之著有問斯對宛若不能言而
訥者非真訥也謙以自處不敢以質而先乎人
當言斯言儼如不能言而默者非真默也畢以
自牧不敢以智而加乎彼是豈矯揉而然哉在
鄉黨自當如此一盛德之符焉至若宗廟朝廷
禮法之所在政事之所出夫子於此也何如便
便以問而欲詢其禮法之詳便便以言而欲審
===
其政事之實問夫禮法而精微委折之不明不
已也謹言所言不敢有所放耳言夫政事
而是非得失之未明不從已也但謹其所發不
敢有所肆耳是豈勉強而然哉在廟朝自當如
此一盛德之隅焉在鄉黨如彼在廟朝如此此
聖人之言貌有以極自然之妙也歟抑者之鄉
黨一篇門人所以記聖人者不止乎此朝聘行
禮衣服飲食以至賜予饋問接人行事之類不
一而足撰不離書而備錄之今讀其書即其事
punctuated: 鄉黨者，父兄之所居，宗族之所聚。夫子於此也何如？爾恭欽容，而恂恂乎信實之形；敦本尚質，而恂恂乎誠慤之著。有問斯對，宛若不能言，而訥者非真訥也，謙以自處，不敢以質而先乎人。當言斯言，儼如不能言，而默者非真默也，畢以自牧，不敢以智而加乎彼。是豈矯揉而然哉？在鄉黨自當如此，一盛德之符焉。至若宗廟朝廷，禮法之所在，政事之所出，夫子於此也何如？便便以問，而欲詢其禮法之詳；便便以言，而欲審其政事之實。問夫禮法，而精微委折之不明不已也，謹言所言，不敢有所放耳。言夫政事，而是非得失之未明不從已也，但謹其所發，不敢有所肆耳。是豈勉強而然哉？在廟朝自當如此，一盛德之隅焉。在鄉黨如彼，在廟朝如此，此聖人之言貌有以極自然之妙也歟？抑者之鄉黨一篇，門人所以記聖人者不止乎此。朝聘行禮，衣服飲食，以至賜予饋問、接人行事之類，不一而足，撰不離書而備錄之。今讀其書，即其事，
translation_en:
…The village community is where fathers and elder brothers dwell and members of the lineage gather. How did the Master conduct himself here? With a respectful bearing [?], his mild and unassuming manner manifested trustworthiness and sincerity; honoring fundamentals and valuing simplicity, that same manner revealed his earnest integrity. When questioned, he answered, seeming almost unable to speak. Yet his apparent inarticulateness was no real inability: he placed himself humbly, not presuming to put himself before others on account of his native qualities. When speech was called for, he spoke, appearing as though unable to speak. Yet his apparent silence was no real reticence: he disciplined himself [?], not presuming to place himself above others on account of his wisdom. Could this have resulted from contrivance? In his village community, this was naturally how he should behave—one manifestation of his abundant virtue.

As for the ancestral temple and the court, where ritual regulations reside and affairs of government originate, how did the Master conduct himself there? He questioned fluently, seeking to inquire into the details of ritual regulations; he spoke fluently, seeking to ascertain the realities of governmental affairs. In asking about ritual regulations, he would not stop until their subtleties and intricate details were clear. He was simply careful about what he said, never daring to speak without restraint. In speaking of governmental affairs, he would not stop [?] until right and wrong, gains and losses, were clear. He was simply cautious in what he uttered, never daring to give himself free rein. Could this have resulted from forced effort? In the temple and at court, this was naturally how he should behave—one aspect of his abundant virtue. Such was his conduct in the village community, and such his conduct in the temple and at court: did not the sage’s speech and bearing thus realize the utmost subtlety of natural spontaneity?

Moreover, in the chapter “Xiangdang” (“The Village Community”) [?], what the disciples recorded of the sage was not confined to this. Court audiences, diplomatic visits, the performance of rites, clothing, food and drink, and even gifts, offerings of food, inquiries after others, dealings with people, and the conduct of affairs—the examples are too numerous to enumerate. They compiled a comprehensive written record of these [?]. Now, reading their book and considering those deeds…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
究然如聖人之捏同也程子謂分明畫出一箇
聖人允信有志於聖者宜潛心焉
君子之中庸也君子而時中　宋洪濂
同考試官□諭□　批　〔作此題者率多牽合補綴殊不愜人意此篇明白簡當讀之令人痛快〕
同考試官教諭毛　批　〔中庸二題理學難作此篇體認親切鋪敘典則宜錄出〕
===
考試官□教□　批　〔理學如此篇明白拭目〕
考試官教□□　批　〔兼體用說最是〕
中庸中明君子能□□□道以其德之備而行之
宜也夫德之備行之宜則其體用全矣君子所
以能體道者固如此試嘗□思子為道學之憂
而作中庸此則引孔子之言以釋首章之義謂
夫中庸者不偏不倚無過不及而平常之理乃
天命所當然精微之極致是中庸也雖曰衆人
所同具而得焉者寡惟君子為能體之而與中
punctuated:
究然如聖人之捏同也。程子謂：「分明畫出一箇聖人。」允信！有志於聖者，宜潛心焉。

君子之中庸也，君子而時中。　宋洪濂

同考試官□諭□批〔作此題者率多牽合補綴，殊不愜人意。此篇明白簡當，讀之令人痛快。〕
同考試官教諭毛批〔中庸二題，理學難作。此篇體認親切，鋪敘典則，宜錄出。〕
考試官□教□批〔理學如此篇，明白拭目。〕
考試官教□□批〔兼體用說，最是。〕

中庸中明君子能□□□道，以其德之備而行之宜也。夫德之備、行之宜，則其體用全矣。君子所以能體道者，固如此。試嘗□思子為道學之憂而作中庸，此則引孔子之言以釋首章之義，謂夫中庸者，不偏不倚、無過不及而平常之理，乃天命所當然、精微之極致。是中庸也，雖曰衆人所同具，而得焉者寡，惟君子為能體之而與中
translation_en:
…as though in the sage’s very presence [?]. Master Cheng said: “It distinctly portrays a sage.” How true! Those who aspire to sagehood should devote themselves to its study.

“The gentleman’s practice of the Mean consists in being a gentleman and keeping to the Mean as circumstances require.” — Song Honglian

Comment by Associate Examiner □, an Instructor [?]: “Those who write on this topic generally force connections and patch arguments together, with thoroughly unsatisfactory results. This essay is clear, concise, and apt; reading it is immensely gratifying.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Instructor: “For the two topics from the Doctrine of the Mean, essays on the learning of principle are difficult to compose. This essay shows an intimate grasp of the subject, and its exposition follows exemplary standards. It should be selected for inclusion.”
Comment by the Examiner whose title and name are partly illegible: “An essay on the learning of principle like this one is clear and opens the eyes [?].”
Comment by the Examiner whose title and name are partly illegible: “Explaining both substance and function is exactly right.”

The Doctrine of the Mean makes clear that the gentleman can … the Way [?] because his virtue is complete and his conduct appropriate. When virtue is complete and conduct appropriate, substance and function are both fully realized. This is indeed how the gentleman can embody the Way. Let us consider how Zisi [?], concerned for the learning of the Way, composed the Doctrine of the Mean. Here he quotes Confucius to explain the meaning of the opening chapter. The Mean is the constant principle that inclines to neither side, deviates in neither direction, and involves neither excess nor deficiency. It is what the mandate of Heaven requires, the utmost refinement and subtlety. Although this Mean is said to be equally inherent in everyone, few attain it. Only the gentleman can embody it and become one with the Mean …

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
庸爲一焉雖曰衆人所同有而昧焉者多惟君
子爲能體之而與中庸無二焉君子之所以爲
中庸者何哉蓋其戒愼之誠每懸於念慮而預
存天理之本然者以周是以君子之德渾然備
於己而無或虧也恐懼之誠常在於思惟而預
養天理之本然者以至是以君子之德粹然有
於我而不或欠也此則不偏不倚而中庸之體
立矣不寧惟是又能隨時以處中事有千變□
各當其可時不同而中亦不同未嘗膠柱適莫
===
之見以泥於中焉因時以用中行有萬殊而均
適其宜時有異而中亦有異未嘗執拳可否之
論以拘於中焉此則無過不及而中庸之用行
矣吁動靜不違體用兼備體道者之能事尚何
有餘蘊哉大抵天下之道至聖人而止聖人之
道至中庸而止然豈易知易行哉必知仁勇之
兼備斯可矣若知賢之過愚不肖之不及亦安
望其道之明且行哉子思子爲此懼故述所聞
父師之意以立言而此則又引夫子之言以發
punctuated: 庸爲一焉。雖曰衆人所同有，而昧焉者多，惟君子爲能體之，而與中庸無二焉。君子之所以爲中庸者何哉？蓋其戒愼之誠，每懸於念慮，而預存天理之本然者以周，是以君子之德渾然備於己而無或虧也。恐懼之誠，常在於思惟，而預養天理之本然者以至，是以君子之德粹然有於我而不或欠也。此則不偏不倚，而中庸之體立矣。不寧惟是，又能隨時以處中，事有千變□各當其可，時不同而中亦不同，未嘗膠柱適莫之見以泥於中焉。因時以用中，行有萬殊而均適其宜，時有異而中亦有異，未嘗執拳可否之論以拘於中焉。此則無過不及，而中庸之用行矣。吁！動靜不違，體用兼備，體道者之能事尚何有餘蘊哉？大抵天下之道至聖人而止，聖人之道至中庸而止。然豈易知易行哉？必知仁勇之兼備斯可矣。若知賢之過，愚不肖之不及，亦安望其道之明且行哉？子思子爲此懼，故述所聞父師之意以立言，而此則又引夫子之言以發
translation_en:
…and become one with the Mean. Although it is something all people possess in common, many remain ignorant of it; only the gentleman can embody it and be wholly at one with it. How is it that the gentleman realizes the Mean? His sincere vigilance is ever present in his thoughts, and his advance preservation of Heavenly principle in its original state is thorough. Thus the gentleman’s virtue is fully complete within himself, without any impairment. His sincere apprehension is constantly present in his reflections, and his advance nurturing of Heavenly principle in its original state is consummate. Thus the gentleman’s virtue exists purely within himself, without any deficiency. In this way, inclining neither to one side nor the other, the substance of the Mean is established.
Nor is this all. He can also abide in the mean according to the circumstances of each moment. Affairs undergo a thousand changes, [illegible] each meeting what is fitting. As the circumstances differ, so does the mean. He never rigidly adheres to fixed views of favoring or rejecting something, thereby becoming inflexible about the mean. He applies the mean according to the circumstances. Actions differ in ten thousand ways, yet all accord with what is appropriate. As the circumstances vary, so does the mean. He never clings obstinately [?] to judgments of approval or disapproval, thereby constraining the mean. In this way, with neither excess nor deficiency, the functioning of the Mean is put into practice.
Ah! In activity and stillness alike there is no deviation, and substance and function are both complete. What further potential could remain unrealized in the achievement of one who embodies the Way? Generally speaking, the Way of all under Heaven reaches its culmination in the sage, and the Way of the sage reaches its culmination in the Mean. Yet how could it be easy to understand or easy to practice? Only when wisdom, benevolence, and courage are all fully present is this possible. If the wise and worthy go too far, while the foolish and unworthy fall short, how could one hope that this Way would be understood and practiced? Master Zisi feared this, and therefore set forth the purport of what he had heard from his father and teacher to formulate his teaching. Here he further quotes the Master’s words to elucidate…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
明之其欲人之體道也切矣嗚呼夐之濂鹿
遠朱子真知子思者歟
以君命將之再拜稽首而受其後廩人繼
粟庖人繼肉不以君命將之
何景明
同考試官訓導林　批　作孟子義要有孟
子文氣此篇得之他日用世必能成英俊事業
同考試官教諭王　批　不襲故語而皆新
意自有動人處偶得此篇於衆作中真若連
===
日啖菜茹而忽嗜膾炙咀嚼不能下嚥
考試官教授李　批　發明國君養賢之禮
無餘蘊當是作手
考試官教授濮　批　理明詞暢錄之
大賢論國君之養賢當曲盡其禮也蓋不以命
餽則慢而數以命餽則勞也然則既於前而絡
於後固君養賢之禮豈復有餘法哉昔者孟子
因萬章之問而告之以此謂夫人君既有以悅
乎賢者必有以養乎賢者養之宜何如如食必
punctuated:
明之，其欲人之體道也切矣。嗚呼！夐之濂鹿遠，朱子真知子思者歟？

以君命將之，再拜稽首而受。其後廩人繼粟，庖人繼肉，不以君命將之。

何景明

同考試官訓導林，批：作孟子義，要有孟子文氣，此篇得之。他日用世，必能成英俊事業。

同考試官教諭王，批：不襲故語，而皆新意，自有動人處。偶得此篇於衆作中，真若連日啖菜茹，而忽嗜膾炙，咀嚼不能下嚥。

考試官教授李，批：發明國君養賢之禮，無餘蘊，當是作手。

考試官教授濮，批：理明詞暢，錄之。

大賢論國君之養賢，當曲盡其禮也。蓋不以命餽則慢，而數以命餽則勞也。然則既於前而絡於後，固君養賢之禮，豈復有餘法哉？昔者孟子因萬章之問而告之以此，謂夫人君既有以悅乎賢者，必有以養乎賢者。養之宜何如？如食必
translation_en:
…to elucidate it. How earnest was his desire that people should embody the Way! Alas! [The phrase 夐之濂鹿遠 is unclear.] Was Master Zhu not one who truly understood Zisi?

“Present it in the ruler’s name, and he bows twice, touching his forehead to the ground, and accepts it. Thereafter, the granary keeper continues to supply grain and the cook continues to supply meat, without presenting them in the ruler’s name.”

He Jingming

Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor, comments: “An exposition of the meaning of the Mencius must possess the literary vigor of Mencius himself. This essay achieves it. When its author enters public service in the future, he will surely accomplish the deeds of an outstanding talent.”

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “It does not imitate familiar expressions; its ideas are all fresh and have an inherently moving quality. Coming upon this essay among the many submissions was truly like eating vegetables for days on end and then suddenly savoring sliced meat and roast meat—chewing them and unable to bring oneself to swallow.”

Examiner Li, Professor, comments: “It elucidates the rites by which a ruler supports worthy men, leaving nothing unexplored. Its author must be an accomplished writer.”

Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: “The principles are clear and the language flows freely. Accept it.”

The great worthy, in discussing a ruler’s support of worthy men, held that every detail of the proper rites should be fulfilled. For to send provisions without a command in the ruler’s name would be disrespectful, while repeatedly sending them with such a command would be burdensome. Thus, to do so at the outset and maintain the connection thereafter [?] is precisely the proper rite by which a ruler supports worthy men. What further procedure could there be? In former times, Mencius explained this in response to Wan Zhang’s question. His meaning was that, once a ruler has the means to please worthy men, he must also have the means to support them. How should he support them? For example, for food one must…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
用粟也初以君命將其粟寵光俯臨於舍館而
繙衣之好有加殺必用肉也初以君命將其肉
恩榮旁燭乎鼎俎而杕杜之愛無已君餽如此
為之賢者必再拜稽首對荅於登嘉之頃于以
昭君命之寵光而罔敢以或違稽顙再拜欽肅
於來餽之時于以承君惠之恩榮而罔敢以或
怠自是而後粟或無也廩人之掌粟者自以常
職而繼之粟所謂每食無餘無有焉或無也
庖人之司肉者自以常職而繼之肉所謂每食
===
不飽無有焉夫廩人繼粟則其餽不以君命為
辭矣所以然者非簡也正欲賢者免再拜之勤
耳庖人繼肉則其餽不以君命為名矣所以然
者非慢也不欲賢者有亟拜之勞耳吁國君養
賢之禮如此繆公亟致鼎肉之餽以勞僕僕之
拜子思摽使者之出而讓以犬馬之畜不亦宜
哉抑考易曰大亨以養聖賢聖賢之貴養也明
矣觀繆公之于子思不可不謂之養也但未盡
養之之道耳故孟子之並此論以為養賢之法
punctuated: 用粟也，初以君命將其粟，寵光俯臨於舍館，而繙衣之好有加。殺必用肉也，初以君命將其肉，恩榮旁燭乎鼎俎，而杕杜之愛無已。君餽如此為之，賢者必再拜稽首，對荅於登嘉之頃，于以昭君命之寵光，而罔敢以或違；稽顙再拜，欽肅於來餽之時，于以承君惠之恩榮，而罔敢以或怠。自是而後，粟或無也，廩人之掌粟者自以常職而繼之粟，所謂每食無餘，無有焉。或無也，庖人之司肉者自以常職而繼之肉，所謂每食不飽，無有焉。夫廩人繼粟，則其餽不以君命為辭矣。所以然者，非簡也，正欲賢者免再拜之勤耳。庖人繼肉，則其餽不以君命為名矣。所以然者，非慢也，不欲賢者有亟拜之勞耳。吁！國君養賢之禮如此，繆公亟致鼎肉之餽，以勞僕僕之拜，子思摽使者之出，而讓以犬馬之畜，不亦宜哉？抑考《易》曰：「大亨以養聖賢。」聖賢之貴養也明矣。觀繆公之于子思，不可不謂之養也，但未盡養之之道耳。故孟子之並此論，以為養賢之法……
translation_en:
…grain must be used. At first, the grain is delivered in the ruler’s name: his gracious favor descends upon the worthy man’s lodging, and the affection expressed in “Fan yi” [?; perhaps “Black Robes,” a poem in the Book of Odes] grows still greater. For slaughter [?], meat must be used. At first, the meat is delivered in the ruler’s name: his gracious bounty shines upon the cauldrons and sacrificial stands, and the love expressed in “The Solitary Pear Tree” knows no end. When the ruler presents gifts in this fashion, the worthy man must bow twice and touch his head to the ground, responding as he receives the fine gifts [?]. In this way he makes manifest the honor of the ruler’s command, never daring to disregard it. He knocks his forehead to the ground and bows twice, reverent and solemn when the gifts arrive, thereby receiving the gracious honor of the ruler’s bounty, never daring to be negligent.

Thereafter, if grain runs out, the granary officer responsible for grain replenishes it as part of his regular duties. Thus there is no question of a meal without grain to spare. If supplies run out, the cook responsible for meat replenishes the meat as part of his regular duties. Thus there is no question of a meal that leaves the recipient hungry. When the granary officer replenishes the grain, he no longer presents the gift with words invoking the ruler’s command. This is not a matter of neglect: it is precisely to spare the worthy man the exertion of bowing twice. When the cook replenishes the meat, he no longer presents the gift in the ruler’s name. This is not a matter of disrespect: it is to spare the worthy man the trouble of repeated bows.

Ah! Such are the rites by which the ruler of a state provides for worthy men. Duke Mu repeatedly sent gifts of cooked meat in cauldrons, burdening Zisi with the wearying task of bowing again and again. Was it not fitting that Zisi waved the messenger out and reproached the duke for keeping him as one would a dog or horse?

Furthermore, consulting the Book of Changes, we find: “Great success, through nourishing sages and worthies.” Clearly, nourishing sages and worthies is highly valued. Looking at Duke Mu’s treatment of Zisi, one cannot deny that he provided for him; he simply failed to fulfill the proper way of doing so. Therefore, Mencius brought this discussion together [?] to establish a method for providing for worthy men…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
□下文併以尊賢為言為人君者苟能交盡其
道則太平之業豈可勝言哉噫能養能舉悅賢
之至也唯堯之於舜為能盡之
易
庸言之信庸行之謹閑邪存其誠
閻禮
同考試官教諭孟　批〔九二乃龍德中正之聖人動容周旋自中乎禮初不待於學而能也學者講貫不明往往以用功立說殊失〕
===
同考試官教諭毛　批〔題不難於達辭而難於識理此作兩得之其積學有待者歟〕
〔本旨此篇獨達衆見故錄之〕
考試官教授李　批〔工於說理老筆也〕
考試官教授濮　批〔簡潔得旨〕
德極其盛而持守尤嚴九二大人然也夫庸言
亦信庸行亦謹德極其盛矣而持守之嚴猶不
能已焉非九二大人其孰能之哉文言申乾九
二象傳之意謂夫九二大人雖未得君人之位
punctuated:
□下文併以尊賢為言。為人君者苟能交盡其道，則太平之業豈可勝言哉！噫！能養能舉，悅賢之至也，唯堯之於舜為能盡之。

易
「庸言之信，庸行之謹，閑邪存其誠。」
閻禮

同考試官教諭孟批〔九二乃龍德中正之聖人，動容周旋自中乎禮，初不待於學而能也。學者講貫不明，往往以用功立說，殊失〕
同考試官教諭毛批〔題不難於達辭，而難於識理。此作兩得之，其積學有待者歟？〕
〔本旨。此篇獨達衆見，故錄之。〕
考試官教授李批〔工於說理，老筆也。〕
考試官教授濮批〔簡潔得旨。〕

德極其盛，而持守尤嚴，九二大人然也。夫庸言亦信，庸行亦謹，德極其盛矣，而持守之嚴猶不能已焉。非九二大人，其孰能之哉？《文言》申乾九二《象傳》之意，謂夫九二大人雖未得君人之位
translation_en:
…□[?] The following passage also speaks of honoring the worthy. If a ruler can fully discharge both duties, how could the achievements of his peaceful rule be adequately described? Ah! To nourish the worthy and to raise them to office is the utmost expression of delight in them. Only Yao, in his treatment of Shun, fully accomplished this.

Book of Changes
“Trustworthy in ordinary speech and careful in ordinary conduct, he guards against depravity and preserves his sincerity.”
Yan Li

Comment by Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor: 〔The nine in the second place represents a sage whose dragon virtue is central and correct. His every movement and action naturally accords with ritual propriety; his ability does not depend upon learning. Students fail to understand this clearly through study and discussion, and often base their explanations on deliberate effort, gravely missing…〕
Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Instructor: 〔The difficulty of this topic lies not in expressing oneself clearly, but in understanding its principle. This composition succeeds in both. Is its author one whose accumulated learning awaits an opportunity?〕
〔…the fundamental purport. This essay alone attains an understanding beyond common views; hence it has been recorded.〕 [This annotation continues Meng’s comment above.]
Comment by Examiner Li, Professor: 〔Skillful in explaining principles: the work of a seasoned writer.〕
Comment by Examiner Pu, Professor: 〔Concise and clear, it grasps the essential meaning.〕

His virtue reaches its fullest flourishing, yet his vigilance in maintaining it is especially strict: such is the great man represented by the nine in the second place. Trustworthy even in ordinary speech and careful even in ordinary conduct, his virtue has reached its fullest flourishing; nevertheless, he cannot cease his strict vigilance in maintaining it. Who but the great man of the nine in the second place could achieve this? The Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) elaborates the meaning of the Commentary on the Images (Xiangzhuan) for the nine in the second place of Qian, saying that although this great man has not yet attained the position of ruler over others…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
而已備君人之德是故庸言必忽孰能信之夫
人德極其盛故凡發於言者雖荅述之常自無
不信初不以庸言而有忽所謂口無擇言是已
况加乎民者有不信哉庸行易怠孰能謹之大
人德極其至故凡形於身者雖周旋之微自無
不謹初不以庸行而有怠所謂身無擇行是已
况見乎遠者有不謹哉盛德之至如此純一之
天固無非僻之可干矣大人之心檢身若不及
曷甞謂已信而忘其自保乎邪不必防也而過
===
防之于以存固有之誠使吾之純一者常純一
而不雜焉真實之地固無外誘之可至矣而大
人之心望道如未見曷甞謂已謹而忽其自守
乎私不必禁也而猶禁之于以存本然之誠使
吾之真實者恒真實而不妄焉噫德之至既有
以著其善於外保之嚴又有全其善於中此九
二君德之所以利見也歟抑論之易者理學
之宗乾坤又易學之宗也夫子文言於乾九二
則曰存誠於坤六二則曰敬以直內盖誠者天
punctuated: 而已備君人之德。是故庸言必忽，孰能信之？夫人德極其盛，故凡發於言者，雖荅述之常，自無不信，初不以庸言而有忽，所謂口無擇言是已。况加乎民者，有不信哉？庸行易怠，孰能謹之？大人德極其至，故凡形於身者，雖周旋之微，自無不謹，初不以庸行而有怠，所謂身無擇行是已。况見乎遠者，有不謹哉？盛德之至如此，純一之天固無非僻之可干矣。大人之心，檢身若不及，曷甞謂已信而忘其自保乎？邪不必防也，而過防之，于以存固有之誠，使吾之純一者常純一而不雜焉。真實之地固無外誘之可至矣，而大人之心，望道如未見，曷甞謂已謹而忽其自守乎？私不必禁也，而猶禁之，于以存本然之誠，使吾之真實者恒真實而不妄焉。噫！德之至既有以著其善於外，保之嚴又有全其善於中，此九二君德之所以利見也歟？抑論之，《易》者理學之宗，乾坤又易學之宗也。夫子《文言》於乾九二則曰存誠，於坤六二則曰敬以直內。盖誠者天
translation_en:
…yet already possesses the virtue needed to rule others. Thus, ordinary words are invariably treated carelessly [?]; who can be trustworthy in them? That person's virtue [?] has reached its fullest flourishing. Hence whatever he expresses in words, even commonplace replies and statements, is invariably trustworthy. He never treats words carelessly because they are ordinary. This is what is meant by saying that his mouth utters no words that need to be selected out. How much less could anything he pronounces upon the people be untrustworthy? In ordinary conduct it is easy to grow remiss; who can be circumspect in it? The great man's virtue has reached its utmost perfection. Hence whatever takes bodily form in his conduct, even the smallest movement in his dealings with others, is invariably circumspect. He never grows remiss because an action is ordinary. This is what is meant by saying that his person performs no actions that need to be selected out. How much less could conduct manifest to those far away lack circumspection?

Such is the perfection of his flourishing virtue: his pure and undivided heavenly nature surely admits no intrusion of perversity or wrongdoing. Yet the great man examines himself as though he still fell short. When has he ever thought himself already trustworthy and forgotten to safeguard himself? There is no need to guard against evil, yet he guards against it with redoubled care. In this way he preserves the sincerity inherently his, ensuring that what is pure and undivided within him remains always pure and undivided, without admixture. His ground of genuineness surely admits no approach by external temptations. Yet in his heart the great man looks toward the Way as though he had not yet seen it. When has he ever thought himself already circumspect and neglected to watch over himself? There is no need to restrain selfishness, yet he still restrains it. In this way he preserves his original sincerity, ensuring that what is genuine within him remains constantly genuine, without falsity.

Ah! The perfection of his virtue already makes his goodness manifest outwardly, while the strictness of his vigilance also preserves that goodness intact within. Is this not why the ruler's virtue represented by the second nine makes it beneficial to see him? To discuss this further, the Book of Changes is the fountainhead of the learning of principle, and Qian and Kun are in turn the fountainhead of the study of the Changes. In the Commentary on the Words of the Text, the Master says of Qian's second nine, “preserve sincerity,” and of Kun's second six, “use reverence to make the inner self upright.” For sincerity is Heaven…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
遺徵猶地道始於伏羲心畫而萬世理學之所
自出也或者以卜筮小吾易烏足以知易哉
是故履德之基也謙德之柄也復德之本
也恒德之固也損德之脩也益德之
裕也困德之辨也井德之地也巽德
之制也
〔宋汝濂〕
同考試官教諭孟　批〔九卦乃文考反身脩德之事夫子陳之以為萬世法此篇足以〕
〔發之殆學易而有得者歟〕
同考試官教諭毛　批〔題本平易作者率多驗說且文法破碎觀此篇辭理俱到故〕
===
〔録之〕
考試官教授李　批〔組織傳註成文佳作也〕
考試官教授濮　批〔體認親切可取〕
大傳歷陳九卦而各著其為脩德之事也夫易
聖人憂世之書脩德之術備矣非大傳歷陳九
卦而各著之何以知其深哉大傳陳九卦以明
punctuated:
遺徵猶地道，始於伏羲心畫，而萬世理學之所自出也。或者以卜筮小吾易，烏足以知易哉？

是故履，德之基也；謙，德之柄也；復，德之本也；恒，德之固也；損，德之脩也；益，德之裕也；困，德之辨也；井，德之地也；巽，德之制也。
〔宋汝濂〕

同考試官教諭孟　批〔九卦乃文考反身脩德之事，夫子陳之以為萬世法。此篇足以發之，殆學易而有得者歟？〕
同考試官教諭毛　批〔題本平易，作者率多驗說，且文法破碎。觀此篇，辭理俱到，故録之。〕
考試官教授李　批〔組織傳註成文，佳作也。〕
考試官教授濮　批〔體認親切，可取。〕

大傳歷陳九卦，而各著其為脩德之事也。夫易，聖人憂世之書，脩德之術備矣。非大傳歷陳九卦而各著之，何以知其深哉？大傳陳九卦以明
translation_en:
…the surviving traces resemble the Way of Earth [?]. These began with Fuxi’s depiction of his mind in the hexagram lines and are the source from which the learning of principle for all ages proceeds. Some belittle our Book of Changes as mere divination. How could they possibly understand the Changes?

“Thus, Lü (Treading) is the foundation of virtue; Qian (Modesty), the handle of virtue; Fu (Return), the root of virtue; Heng (Constancy), the firmness of virtue; Sun (Decrease), the cultivation of virtue; Yi (Increase), the abundance of virtue; Kun (Oppression), the discernment of virtue; Jing (The Well), the ground of virtue; and Xun (The Gentle), the regulation of virtue.”
〔Song Rulian〕

Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor, comments: 〔The nine hexagrams concern the work of self-examination and the cultivation of virtue undertaken by King Wen [?]. The Master set them forth as a model for all ages. This essay adequately elucidates them. Surely its author has gained some understanding through studying the Changes?〕
Associate Examiner Mao, Instructor, comments: 〔The topic is inherently straightforward, yet most writers produce evidential explanations [?], and their compositions are fragmented. In this essay, both expression and reasoning are fully accomplished; hence its inclusion.〕
Examiner Li, Professor, comments: 〔A fine composition, woven together from the commentaries and annotations.〕
Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: 〔Its understanding is intimate and well grounded, and merits acceptance.〕

The Great Commentary sets forth the nine hexagrams in succession, showing how each concerns the cultivation of virtue. The Changes is a book arising from the sage’s concern for the world; it contains the full range of methods for cultivating virtue. Had the Great Commentary not set forth the nine hexagrams in succession and elucidated each, how could we know their depth? The Great Commentary presents the nine hexagrams to illuminate…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
處憂患之道謂夫處憂患莫要於脩德而脩德
不外乎易書是故履之為卦上天下澤定分不
易為德而非履則流蕩而無所立履其德之基
乎謙之為卦山在地中以卑蘊高為禮而非謙
則驕抗而無所執謙其德之柄乎雷在地中卦
名曰復在人則心不外而善端存所以反求之
者要矣非德之本而何雷風相與卦名曰恒在
人則守不厭而常且久所以自檢之者嚴矣非
德之固而何懲忿窒慾以為德之脩者又必於
===
損而得之蓋以其卦山澤相臨有損之義也遷
善改過以為德之裕者又必於益而得之蓋以
其卦風雷相助有益之義也澤中無水卦名困
也而困之道能通人必處困能亨然後可以驗
其力是困為德之辨焉木上有水卦名井也而
井之體不遷人必自養不變然後可以成其德
是井為德之地焉至若巽者一陰伏於二陽之
下是能巽於理以酌時之宜順於理以制事之
變所以為德之制者有不在於巽乎然九卦之
punctuated: 處憂患之道，謂夫處憂患莫要於脩德，而脩德不外乎易書。是故履之為卦，上天下澤，定分不易。為德而非履，則流蕩而無所立，履其德之基乎？謙之為卦，山在地中，以卑蘊高。為禮而非謙，則驕抗而無所執，謙其德之柄乎？雷在地中，卦名曰復，在人則心不外而善端存，所以反求之者要矣，非德之本而何？雷風相與，卦名曰恒，在人則守不厭而常且久，所以自檢之者嚴矣，非德之固而何？懲忿窒慾，以為德之脩者，又必於損而得之，蓋以其卦山澤相臨，有損之義也。遷善改過，以為德之裕者，又必於益而得之，蓋以其卦風雷相助，有益之義也。澤中無水，卦名困也，而困之道能通，人必處困能亨，然後可以驗其力，是困為德之辨焉。木上有水，卦名井也，而井之體不遷，人必自養不變，然後可以成其德，是井為德之地焉。至若巽者，一陰伏於二陽之下，是能巽於理以酌時之宜，順於理以制事之變，所以為德之制者，有不在於巽乎？然九卦之
translation_en:
…the way to meet sorrow and adversity, explaining that nothing is more essential in meeting sorrow and adversity than cultivating virtue, and that cultivating virtue does not go beyond the Book of Changes. Thus, in the hexagram Treading (Lü), Heaven is above and the Lake below: their allotted positions are fixed and unchanging. If one practices virtue without treading properly, one drifts about with no firm footing. Is not Treading, then, the foundation of virtue? In the hexagram Modesty (Qian), the Mountain lies within the Earth, concealing height in lowliness. If one practices ritual without modesty, one becomes arrogant and defiant, with nothing to hold fast to. Is not Modesty, then, the handle of virtue?

Thunder within the Earth gives the hexagram its name, Return (Fu). In a person, this means that the heart does not stray outward and the beginnings of goodness remain. The means of seeking within oneself are therefore essential. What could this be but the root of virtue? Thunder and Wind act together, giving the hexagram its name, Constancy (Heng). In a person, this means holding fast without weariness, remaining constant and enduring. The means of keeping oneself in check are therefore rigorous. What could this be but the firmness of virtue?

To restrain anger and curb desires, thereby cultivating virtue, one must find the means in Decrease (Sun). This is because its images, Mountain and Lake, stand one above the other and convey the meaning of decrease. To move toward goodness and correct faults, thereby enlarging virtue, one must find the means in Increase (Yi). This is because its images, Wind and Thunder, assist each other and convey the meaning of increase.

A Lake without water gives the hexagram its name, Adversity (Kun). Yet the way of Adversity permits passage through difficulty. Only when a person can meet adversity and still attain success can that person's strength be tested. Thus Adversity is what distinguishes virtue. Water above Wood gives the hexagram its name, the Well (Jing). The Well remains fixed in place. Only when a person nourishes the self without changing can virtue be brought to completion. Thus the Well is the ground of virtue.

As for the Gentle (Xun), one yin line lies beneath two yang lines. This means being able to yield to principle and weigh what is appropriate to the time, and to follow principle in responding to changing circumstances. How could the regulation of virtue lie anywhere but in the Gentle? Yet among the nine hexagrams…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
間析之則各一其事合之則各有其序脩德以
處憂患之道無餘藴矣大抵處順者易為功處
逆者難為力而文王作易適丁憂患之時故以
憂世之心悉寓之易所謂危者使平是也然治
平昌大之道亦何莫而不與哉觀夫井所以勞
民而勸相謙所以稱物而平施履所以辨上下
而定民志也可知已故謂處憂患之道不外乎
易則可謂易之道不外乎處憂患則不可
書
九叙惟歌戒之用休董之用威勸之以九
===
歌
何景明
同考試官訓導林 批 民心和樂形於聲
詠治功之成有足徵者且又足以維持之於
永久題意如此作者多不識往往牽合上下
文貫講此篇認理真切而詞氣醇贍故録之
同考試官教諭王 批 此篇融會蔡傳成
文而有虞君民樂生保治之旨發揮殆盡矣
punctuated:
間，析之則各一其事，合之則各有其序，脩德以處憂患之道無餘藴矣。大抵處順者易為功，處逆者難為力，而文王作易，適丁憂患之時，故以憂世之心悉寓之易，所謂危者使平是也。然治平昌大之道，亦何莫而不與哉？觀夫井所以勞民而勸相，謙所以稱物而平施，履所以辨上下而定民志也，可知已。故謂處憂患之道不外乎易則可，謂易之道不外乎處憂患則不可。
書
九叙惟歌，戒之用休，董之用威，勸之以九歌。
何景明
同考試官訓導林批：民心和樂，形於聲詠，治功之成有足徵者，且又足以維持之於永久。題意如此，作者多不識，往往牽合上下文貫講。此篇認理真切，而詞氣醇贍，故録之。
同考試官教諭王批：此篇融會蔡傳成文，而有虞君民樂生保治之旨，發揮殆盡矣。
translation_en:
…among them, considered separately, each concerns its own matter; considered together, each has its place in the sequence. The way of cultivating virtue to meet anxiety and adversity is thus fully disclosed. Generally, those in favorable circumstances can readily achieve results, while those in adversity find it difficult to exert their strength. When King Wen composed the Changes, he happened to encounter a time of anxiety and adversity; he therefore embodied in the Changes his entire concern for the world. This is what is meant by making those in peril secure. Yet what aspect of the way of peaceful government and flourishing prosperity does it not also encompass? This can be understood by observing how the Well hexagram serves to encourage the people in their labors and urge them to assist one another; how Modesty serves to weigh things and distribute impartially; and how Treading serves to distinguish those above from those below and settle the people's intentions. Thus, one may say that the way of meeting anxiety and adversity does not lie outside the Changes; one may not say that the way of the Changes consists solely in meeting anxiety and adversity.

Book of Documents

“When the nine undertakings are put in order, let them be celebrated in song. Admonish them with favorable words, supervise them with severity, and encourage them with the nine songs.”

He Jingming

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor: The people's harmonious and joyful feelings find expression in song, providing sufficient evidence of accomplished government; moreover, this is sufficient to preserve that achievement for all time. Such is the meaning of the topic. Most writers fail to recognize it and often force connections with the preceding and following passages to produce a continuous exposition. This essay grasps the principle accurately and incisively, and its language and tone are pure and ample. For this reason, it has been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: This essay integrates Cai's Commentary into a coherent composition, expounding almost exhaustively the idea that the ruler and people of Youyu delighted in life and preserved good government.

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
潛心理經而有得者
考試官教授李　批　撰寫大禹告君養民
之政詞整理明聽如親立虞廷之上而聞謦
欬者也允宜高薦
考試官教授濮　批　古之大臣許論氣象
宛然
治功之成也驗諸詩治功之保也歸諸詩甚矣
非治功之成固無以使民詠之歌也然徒治之
以法而不勸之以歌又何以保其治功於永久
===
也哉昔大禹因其言儆戒之道而歎美之及此
意謂善政固在於養民養民莫先於府事然謂
之九叙惟歌果何如耶盖必水火金木土穀財
用之所自出者本於天而各順其理正德利用
厚生人事之所當爲者行於人而不亂其常由
是民享府事之利莫不熙熙乎歌詠於飽食煖
衣之地以樂其生民仰脩和之治莫不洋洋乎
詠歌於綱常倫理之域以遂其性夫如是則養
民之功成矣然民情不必其有常而治功難保
punctuated:
潛心理經而有得者。

考試官教授李批：撰寫大禹告君養民之政，詞整理明，聽如親立虞廷之上而聞謦欬者也，允宜高薦。

考試官教授濮批：古之大臣許論氣象宛然。

治功之成也驗諸詩，治功之保也歸諸詩，甚矣！非治功之成，固無以使民詠之歌也。然徒治之以法而不勸之以歌，又何以保其治功於永久也哉？昔大禹因其言儆戒之道而歎美之及此，意謂善政固在於養民，養民莫先於府事。然謂之「九叙惟歌」，果何如耶？盖必水火金木土穀，財用之所自出者，本於天而各順其理；正德利用厚生，人事之所當爲者，行於人而不亂其常。由是民享府事之利，莫不熙熙乎歌詠於飽食煖衣之地，以樂其生；民仰脩和之治，莫不洋洋乎詠歌於綱常倫理之域，以遂其性。夫如是，則養民之功成矣。然民情不必其有常，而治功難保
translation_en:
…one who has devoted his mind to the principles of the Classics and gained understanding.

Examiner Li, Professor, comments: This account of the policies for nourishing the people that Yu the Great presented to his ruler is orderly in expression and clear in principle. Hearing it is like standing in the court of Yu and hearing his very voice. It certainly merits a high recommendation.

Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: The bearing of an ancient great minister in deliberation [?] is vividly present.

The accomplishment of good government is verified through poetry, and its preservation likewise depends on poetry. How profound this is! Without achievements in government, there would certainly be nothing to inspire the people to sing their praises. Yet if one governs them solely through laws and does not encourage them through song, how can those achievements be preserved forever? In ancient times, Yu the Great, while speaking of the way to admonish and caution, extended his admiring praise to this matter. His meaning was that good government assuredly consists in nourishing the people, and that, in nourishing them, nothing takes precedence over the six resources and the three affairs. But what, precisely, does it mean to say, “The nine are duly ordered, and are celebrated in song”? Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain—the sources of material resources—must each follow their proper principles, grounded in Heaven; rectifying virtue, facilitating use, and enriching livelihood—the proper tasks of human activity—must be carried out among the people without disrupting their constant norms. Thus, enjoying the benefits of these resources and affairs, the people all sing joyfully amid ample food and warm clothing, delighting in their lives. Looking up to a government that cultivates these resources and harmonizes these affairs, they all sing exuberantly within the bounds of the cardinal relationships and moral principles, thereby fulfilling their nature. In this way, the work of nourishing the people is accomplished. Yet the dispositions of the people are not necessarily constant, and it is difficult to ensure that the achievements of government…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
其不廢故必民之勤於脩和者則戒勑而休美
之示以今日之勤固善而他日亦當如是也民
之怠於脩和者則督責而懲戒之示以今日之
怠固非而繼此不當仍之也然又以為事之出
於勉强不若感於自然故復即其前日歌詠之
言以勸相之不徒協之律呂而又播之聲音不
惟用之鄉人而且及於邦國以其出於性情者
感乎性情使民必脩必和奮迅踴躍而趨事之
不已也以其詠夫府事者倡乎府事使民益脩
===
益和歡忻鼓舞而赴功之不怠也呵養民治功
之盛允欲保其常盛如此大禹以為帝舜告
聖人之心其不自足如此哉抑考此章大禹誥
明伯益儆戒之謨其曰惟脩惟和惟敘惟歌以
見致治之道必造其極即所謂無虞之時也其
曰戒之董之勸之以見保治之道不一而足即
所謂儆戒之道也古之大臣告君養民之政詳
盡如此此其治之所以不可及也歟
欽時五福用敷錫厥庶民
punctuated:
其不廢。故必民之勤於脩和者，則戒勑而休美之，示以今日之勤固善，而他日亦當如是也；民之怠於脩和者，則督責而懲戒之，示以今日之怠固非，而繼此不當仍之也。然又以為事之出於勉强，不若感於自然，故復即其前日歌詠之言以勸相之。不徒協之律呂，而又播之聲音；不惟用之鄉人，而且及於邦國。以其出於性情者感乎性情，使民必脩必和，奮迅踴躍而趨事之不已也；以其詠夫府事者倡乎府事，使民益脩益和，歡忻鼓舞而赴功之不怠也。呵！養民治功之盛，允欲保其常盛如此。大禹以為帝舜告，聖人之心，其不自足如此哉！抑考此章，大禹誥明伯益儆戒之謨，其曰「惟脩惟和，惟敘惟歌」，以見致治之道必造其極，即所謂無虞之時也；其曰「戒之董之勸之」，以見保治之道不一而足，即所謂儆戒之道也。古之大臣告君養民之政，詳盡如此，此其治之所以不可及也歟！

欽時五福，用敷錫厥庶民。
translation_en:
…that it will not fall into disuse. Thus, those among the people who diligently cultivate the three affairs and harmonize the six resources must be admonished and commended, showing them that their diligence today is indeed good and that they must act likewise in the days to come. Those who are negligent in cultivation and harmonization must be reproved and chastened, showing them that their negligence today is indeed wrong and must not continue thereafter. Yet action undertaken under compulsion is thought inferior to action arising from spontaneous inspiration. Hence the words they previously sang are again used to encourage and assist them. These are not merely harmonized with the pitch standards but also disseminated in song; they are employed not only among the local people but throughout the states. What issues from human nature and feeling moves human nature and feeling, making the people unfailingly cultivate and harmonize, eagerly springing into action and attending to their tasks without cease. Songs celebrating the six resources and three affairs promote those resources and affairs, making the people cultivate and harmonize ever more fully, joyfully stirred to pursue their work without flagging. Ah! Such is the flourishing achievement of government in nourishing the people, and such is the earnest desire to preserve its enduring flourishing. Great Yu presented this as an admonition to Emperor Shun [?]: how little the sage’s heart rested in self-satisfaction!

Furthermore, examining this chapter, we find that Great Yu elucidates Boyi’s counsel concerning vigilance and admonition. His words, “Let them be cultivated and harmonized, ordered and sung,” show that the way to achieve good government must be brought to its utmost perfection: this is precisely what is meant by a time free from anxiety. His words, “Admonish them, supervise them, and encourage them,” show that no single measure suffices to preserve good government: this is precisely what is meant by the way of vigilance and admonition. So comprehensive and thorough were the counsels that the great ministers of antiquity offered their rulers concerning government that nourishes the people. Is this not why their achievements in government cannot be equaled?

Reverently attend to these five blessings, and thereby bestow them widely upon the common people.

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
李希夔
同考試官訓導林　批〔題本平易而作者於敷錫處欠明此篇認理透徹而詞足以發之讀之令人躍然〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔不𡨚不泛而理致明白殆闇於中而肆於外者歟〕
考試官教授濮　批〔詞典而贍可嘉〕
考試官教授李　批〔本建極化民立說良是〕
觀人君建極之效不惟有以厚其身而又有以
===
厚其民蓋君之建極而福集於上有以厚其身
矣以之而溥於民則民其有不厚者乎箕子衍
皇極之疇至此以為人君中天下而立定四海
之民福不期歛也而歛之有其本歛亦易能也
而能之有其道誠能盡人倫之極致全義
當然則有以荷天之休而佑命之惟純嘏
慶而眷命之罔懋不惟富壽而且康寧焉祈
之隆如日之方升不惟攸好德而且考終命焉
福履之成如川之方至從容於九重而休嘉之
punctuated:
李希夔

同考試官訓導林，批〔題本平易，而作者於敷錫處欠明。此篇認理透徹，而詞足以發之，讀之令人躍然。〕
同考試官教諭王，批〔不𡨚不泛，而理致明白，殆闇於中而肆於外者歟？〕
考試官教授濮，批〔詞典而贍，可嘉。〕
考試官教授李，批〔本建極化民立說，良是。〕

觀人君建極之效，不惟有以厚其身，而又有以厚其民。蓋君之建極而福集於上，有以厚其身矣；以之而溥於民，則民其有不厚者乎？箕子衍皇極之疇，至此以為人君中天下而立，定四海之民。福不期歛也，而歛之有其本；歛亦易能也，而能之有其道。誠能盡人倫之極致，全義當然，則有以荷天之休，而佑命之惟純；嘏慶而眷命之罔懋。不惟富壽，而且康寧焉，祈之隆如日之方升；不惟攸好德，而且考終命焉，福履之成如川之方至。從容於九重，而休嘉之
translation_en:
Li Xikui

Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The topic itself is straightforward, yet writers tend to be insufficiently clear about the passage on universally bestowing blessings. This essay penetrates the principle thoroughly, and its language adequately brings it out. Reading it makes one leap with delight.〕
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔Neither strained [?] nor vague, it makes the underlying principles clear. Perhaps this is a case of inward comprehension [?] finding free outward expression?〕
Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: 〔The language is classical and ample: commendable.〕
Examiner Li, Professor, comments: 〔The argument is grounded in establishing the supreme standard and transforming the people. This is entirely sound.〕

Consider the effects of a ruler’s establishing the supreme standard: he thereby enriches not only himself but also his people. For when the ruler establishes the supreme standard and blessings gather above, he has the means to enrich himself. If he then extends these blessings universally to the people, could any of them fail to be enriched? When Jizi elaborates the category of the August Ultimate, at this point his meaning is that the ruler stands at the center of the realm and brings stability to the people within the Four Seas. Blessings are gathered without deliberately seeking to gather them, yet their gathering has a foundation. Gathering them is readily achievable, yet achieving it has its proper way. If he can truly fulfill human relationships to their utmost and fully realize what righteousness requires, he can receive Heaven’s favor, with its protecting mandate wholly pure; its great blessings and favoring mandate are without abundance [?]. There will be not only wealth and longevity but also health and peace, with blessings [?] increasing like the newly rising sun; there will be not only a love of virtue but also the completion of one’s allotted lifespan, with good fortune coming to fulfillment like an arriving river’s flow. At ease within the ninefold palace, while auspicious blessings …

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
來愈盛而不衰矣優游於五位而吉祥之集有
隆而不替矣夫人君集福於上如此豈特自厚
其身而已哉又使天下之民觀感興起化於人
倫之中感動奮發歸於義理之內亦富壽也亦
康寧也而餘慶溥及於八荒亦攸好德也亦考
終命也而利澤廣被於萬姓出以作入以息免
於刑戮而囿乎時叙之天仰以事俯以育無有
遘疾而陶於時雍之地是則君膺福而曰斂者
極建於上而福自來民獲福而曰錫者極建於
===
此而民自化人君建極之效有如此夫抑皇極
一疇乃九疇之樞紐五行之統會能建極於上
則凡有血氣者皆面内環觀有不取則於此而
保之者乎君道所係之重如此故箕子因武王
訪道而陳洪範至此衍皇極之疇而極其詳以
見八疇之理皆為皇極之所以建所以行而治
天下之大經大法無餘藴矣是知箕子非特為
武王告而實為天下萬世告
詩
punctuated:
來愈盛而不衰矣，優游於五位而吉祥之集有隆而不替矣。夫人君集福於上如此，豈特自厚其身而已哉？又使天下之民觀感興起，化於人倫之中；感動奮發，歸於義理之內。亦富壽也，亦康寧也，而餘慶溥及於八荒；亦攸好德也，亦考終命也，而利澤廣被於萬姓。出以作，入以息，免於刑戮而囿乎時叙之天；仰以事，俯以育，無有遘疾而陶於時雍之地。是則君膺福而曰斂者，極建於上而福自來；民獲福而曰錫者，極建於此而民自化。人君建極之效有如此夫！
抑皇極一疇，乃九疇之樞紐，五行之統會。能建極於上，則凡有血氣者皆面内環觀，有不取則於此而保之者乎？君道所係之重如此，故箕子因武王訪道而陳《洪範》，至此衍皇極之疇而極其詳，以見八疇之理皆為皇極之所以建、所以行，而治天下之大經大法無餘藴矣。是知箕子非特為武王告，而實為天下萬世告。
詩
translation_en:
…the blessings that come grow ever more abundant and never decline. Dwelling at ease in the fifth position—the ruler’s place—he sees auspicious blessings gather in increasing abundance without diminution. When the ruler thus gathers blessings above, how could he merely enrich himself alone? He also causes the people throughout the realm to be moved by his example and stirred to emulation, transformed within the human relationships; inspired and roused to effort, they return to moral rightness and principle. They too enjoy wealth and longevity, and health and peace, while blessings overflow to the eight remotest regions. They too love virtue and complete their allotted lifespan, while benefits and bounty spread widely among all the people. Going out to work and returning home to rest, they escape punishment and execution and live beneath a heaven where all is duly ordered. Serving their elders above and nurturing their children below, they suffer no illness and are nurtured in a land of prevailing harmony. Thus, when the ruler receives blessings, this is called “gathering”: the supreme standard is established above, and blessings come of themselves. When the people obtain blessings, this is called “bestowing”: the supreme standard is established here, and the people are transformed of themselves. Such are the effects of the ruler’s establishment of the supreme standard!
Now, the category of the Sovereign’s Supreme Standard is the pivot of the nine categories and the point at which the Five Phases are brought together. If the ruler can establish this standard above, all living people will turn inward toward him and look upon him from every side. Could any fail to take their rule from it and hold fast to it? Such is the weight of what depends upon the ruler’s Way. Hence, when King Wu inquired about the Way, Jizi set forth the Great Plan. On reaching this point, he expounded the category of the Sovereign’s Supreme Standard in the fullest detail, showing that the principles of the other eight categories are all the means by which the Sovereign’s Supreme Standard is established and put into practice. Thus nothing remained unexpressed of the great guiding principles and laws for governing the realm. From this we know that Jizi spoke not only for King Wu, but indeed for all the world through ten thousand generations.
Classic of Poetry

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
王猶允塞徐方既來徐方既同天子之功
四方既平徐方來庭徐方不回王曰
還歸
李東熙
同考試官訓導郭　批〔反覆其詞以歸功〕〔於天子朱傳明白有以王曰還歸一句剔出〕
作班師之命為𣪍者絲於本旨
同考試官學正李　批〔作文氣勢如鵰鶚〕〔得秋風便當上次霄漢通篇入彀無恭不知〕
===
考試官教授李　批〔講王道服遠前後照〕〔他房有能頡頏未〕
應得反覆意思
考試官教授濮　批〔作大雅義如此者不〕〔多見當錄出〕
詩人反覆以王道服遠歸其功於君焉蓋王道
甚大而遠方懷之非獨兵威然也詩人反覆其
詞而歸其功於君其寓意深矣昔宣王自將以
伐淮北之夷詩人美之至此若曰威天下不以
punctuated:
王猶允塞，徐方既來。徐方既同，天子之功。四方既平，徐方來庭。徐方不回，王曰：「還歸。」
李東熙。
同考試官訓導郭，批〔反覆其詞以歸功〕〔於天子，朱傳明白。有以王曰還歸一句剔出〕作班師之命，為𣪍者絲於本旨。
同考試官學正李，批〔作文氣勢如鵰鶚〕〔得秋風，便當上次霄漢。通篇入彀，無恭不知〕。
考試官教授李，批〔講王道服遠，前後照〕〔他房有能頡頏未〕應，得反覆意思。
考試官教授濮，批〔作大雅義如此者不〕〔多見，當錄出〕。
詩人反覆以王道服遠，歸其功於君焉。蓋王道甚大，而遠方懷之，非獨兵威然也。詩人反覆其詞，而歸其功於君，其寓意深矣。昔宣王自將以伐淮北之夷，詩人美之。至此，若曰：「威天下不以
translation_en:
“The king’s plans were truly fulfilled; the people of Xu had come in submission. The people of Xu were now united: this was the Son of Heaven’s achievement. The four quarters were pacified; the people of Xu came to court. The people of Xu did not turn away. The king said, ‘Return home.’”
Li Dongxi.
Associate Examiner Guo, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The repeated phrasing attributes the achievement to the Son of Heaven. Zhu Xi’s commentary is clear. Some single out the phrase ‘The king said, “Return home”’ as an order to bring the army back; those who interpret it thus [the concluding judgment is garbled: 為𣪍者絲於本旨][?].”
Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “The momentum of this composition resembles an eagle or osprey catching the autumn wind: it should at once ascend to the heavens [?]. The entire piece hits the mark; [the concluding phrase 無恭不知 is garbled][?].”
Examiner Li, Professor, comments: “In explaining how the Kingly Way wins the submission of distant peoples, the earlier and later passages echo each other, capturing the sense of the repeated phrasing.” An interposed annotation asks: “Is there anything in the other examination rooms that can rival it?”
Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: “Interpretations of the Greater Odes as good as this are seldom seen. It should be selected for inclusion in the record.”
The poet repeatedly attributes to the ruler the achievement of winning the submission of distant peoples through the Kingly Way. For the Kingly Way is exceedingly great, and distant peoples cherish it; military might alone does not produce this result. The poet repeats his words and attributes the achievement to the ruler: the meaning he conveys is profound indeed. Formerly, King Xuan personally led an expedition against the Yi peoples north of the Huai River, and the poet praised him. At this point, it is as though he were saying: “To overawe all under Heaven does not depend upon …

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
兵革之利服夷狄不在征伐也動擧我周王勵
志中興光復舊物以實德代萬國而不專倚衍
小大遐邇一此德之流通王道何蕩蕩也以誠
心臨蒞事而無事虛文禮樂征伐一此心之敷
布王道何平平也是以徐方之夷雖嘗背叛也
今則聞風而來歸矣雖嘗渙離也今則率衆而
來同矣來非畏威懷王道而來赫赫天子有此
元功也將帥何預焉同非懼殺懷王道而同明
明天子有此駿功也臣鄰無力焉夫叛者既服
===
四方共覩安靖之休亂者既平四方自無繹騷
之患然徐方不徒來也稱藩君門悉囿於王道
之中尚何敢弗庭乎徐方不但同也甘心臣節
相忘於王道之内尚何敢復違乎吾王於此亦
惟曰徐方來歸兵不可窮也萬乘之師可以反
旆還矣淮墳豈久處之地哉徐方來同武不可
黷也六飛之衆可以卷甲歸矣徐土豈遲留之
境哉詩人反覆言之如此豈非欲其不事兵威
而專尚王道發美之中寓規戒之意也歟抑論
punctuated: 兵革之利，服夷狄不在征伐也。動擧我周王勵志中興，光復舊物，以實德代萬國，而不專倚衍，小大遐邇，一此德之流通，王道何蕩蕩也！以誠心臨蒞事，而無事虛文，禮樂征伐，一此心之敷布，王道何平平也！是以徐方之夷，雖嘗背叛也，今則聞風而來歸矣；雖嘗渙離也，今則率衆而來同矣。來非畏威，懷王道而來，赫赫天子有此元功也，將帥何預焉？同非懼殺，懷王道而同，明明天子有此駿功也，臣鄰無力焉。夫叛者既服，四方共覩安靖之休；亂者既平，四方自無繹騷之患。然徐方不徒來也，稱藩君門，悉囿於王道之中，尚何敢弗庭乎？徐方不但同也，甘心臣節，相忘於王道之内，尚何敢復違乎？吾王於此亦惟曰：「徐方來歸，兵不可窮也，萬乘之師可以反旆還矣，淮墳豈久處之地哉？徐方來同，武不可黷也，六飛之衆可以卷甲歸矣，徐土豈遲留之境哉？」詩人反覆言之如此，豈非欲其不事兵威，而專尚王道，發美之中寓規戒之意也歟？抑論
translation_en:
…the advantage of weapons and armor; bringing the Yi and Di into submission does not depend on punitive campaigns. In his actions [?], our king of Zhou resolved to restore the dynasty and recover its former heritage. Through substantial virtue he dealt with the myriad states [?], without relying exclusively on … [?]. Among great and small, far and near, this same virtue circulated: how expansive was the Kingly Way! With a sincere heart he attended to affairs, without resorting to empty formalities. Rites, music, and punitive campaigns were all expressions of this same heart: how even and orderly was the Kingly Way! Thus, although the Yi of the Xu region had formerly rebelled, now, hearing of his influence, they came to give their allegiance. Although they had formerly scattered and withdrawn, now they led their multitudes to join him. They came not from fear of his might, but out of attachment to the Kingly Way. This great achievement belonged to the illustrious Son of Heaven: what part did the commanders have in it? They joined him not from fear of slaughter, but out of attachment to the Kingly Way. This mighty achievement belonged to the enlightened Son of Heaven; his ministers and close attendants contributed no power to it.

Once the rebels had submitted, all four quarters witnessed the blessings of peace and security. Once the disorderly had been pacified, all four quarters were naturally free from the danger of continuing turmoil [?]. Yet the Xu region did more than merely come: its people declared themselves vassals at the ruler’s gate, all encompassed within the Kingly Way. How could they still dare fail to attend his court? The Xu region did more than merely join him: its people willingly observed the duties of subjects, dwelling so naturally within the Kingly Way that distinctions were forgotten. How could they dare defy him again? At this point our king would simply say: “The Xu region has come to give allegiance; warfare must not be pursued to exhaustion. The army of the ruler of ten thousand chariots may turn its banners and return. Are the banks of the Huai a place to remain for long? The Xu region has come to join us; military force must not be used wantonly. The host accompanying the swift six-horse royal chariot may roll up its armor and return. Is the land of Xu a place in which to linger?”

The poet speaks repeatedly in this way. Is this not because he wishes the king to refrain from relying on military might and to esteem the Kingly Way alone, embedding admonition and warning within his praise? Moreover, to discuss…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
樂成之道若舞干而苗格因壘而崇降舜文其
上也次于陘而屈完盟會蕭魚而鄭不叛其次
則齊桓晉悼是也宣王之勝徐則亦桓悼之師
耳而詩人推而納諸舜文之域傳所謂因以爲
戒者有焉嗚呼美不忘矧頌而不諂其常武詩
人之謂乎
烈文辟公錫茲祉福惠我無疆子孫保之
無封靡于爾邦維王其崇之念茲戎
功繼序其皇之無競維人四方其訓
之不顯維德百辟其刑之於乎前王
不忘
===
杜昌
同考試官訓導郭　批　管弦之音而文章
欲近之斯其難矣此作形容功言之意殆盡
同考試官學正李　批　詩有六義故體製
真佳作也
不同爲文不能一例此篇得作頌文之體不
獨明音訓文義而已者故錄之
punctuated:
樂成之道，若舞干而苗格，因壘而崇降，舜、文其上也；次于陘而屈完盟，會蕭魚而鄭不叛，其次則齊桓、晉悼是也。宣王之勝徐，則亦桓、悼之師耳，而詩人推而納諸舜、文之域，傳所謂因以爲戒者有焉。嗚呼！美不忘矧，頌而不諂，其《常武》詩人之謂乎！
烈文辟公，錫茲祉福。惠我無疆，子孫保之。無封靡于爾邦，維王其崇之。念茲戎功，繼序其皇之。無競維人，四方其訓之。不顯維德，百辟其刑之。於乎！前王不忘。
杜昌
同考試官訓導郭，批：管弦之音，而文章欲近之，斯其難矣！此作形容功言之意殆盡。
同考試官學正李，批：詩有六義，故體製——真佳作也——不同，爲文不能一例。此篇得作頌文之體，不獨明音訓文義而已者，故錄之。
translation_en:
…As for the way to celebrate an achievement, Shun and King Wen stand highest: through a dance with shields the Miao submitted, and through encampments Chong surrendered [?]. Next come Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Dao of Jin: encamping at Xing brought Qu Wan to conclude a covenant, and meeting at Xiaoyu kept Zheng from rebelling. King Xuan’s victory over Xu was likewise merely a campaign of the sort conducted by Huan and Dao. Yet the poet elevated it into the realm of Shun and King Wen. Here we find what the commentary calls taking the occasion to offer an admonition. Alas! Praising without forgetting admonition [?], and offering eulogy without flattery—is this not what may be said of the poet of “Ever Martial” (Changwu)?

“Distinguished and Cultured” (Liewen)
Distinguished and cultured, you lords,
You bestow these blessings and good fortune.
Your kindness to us knows no bounds;
May our descendants preserve it.
Do not exact excessive gain or squander resources in your states;
The king will exalt you.
Remember this great achievement;
Your successors shall magnify it.
Nothing rivals worthy men:
The four quarters will follow their teaching.
How illustrious is virtue:
The hundred lords will take it as their model.
Ah! The former kings are not forgotten.

Du Chang.

Associate Examiner Guo, Assistant Instructor, comments: “For prose to approach the sound of pipes and strings—how difficult this is! This work conveys almost exhaustively the meaning of the words concerning achievement [?].”

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “Poetry has six principles, and therefore its forms differ; writing cannot follow a single pattern. This piece captures the form appropriate to a eulogy, going beyond merely elucidating pronunciation, glosses, and textual meaning. It has therefore been selected for inclusion.” The transcribed text inserts “Truly a fine work!” between “its forms” and “differ”; its placement is uncertain [?].

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
考試官教授李　批　文體不類時作則樣
力過人遠矣錄之爲經生式
考試官教授濮　批　得工歌獻頌之體
王者歸諸侯助祭之功而示以報功之意尤必
戒勉之也夫臣有功君固當報之也然又必有
以戒勉之焉其愛人以德之意何如哉此祭於
宗廟而獻助祭諸侯之樂歌謂夫顧此烈文之
辟公相我宗廟之祀事方其對越在天而介我
以繁祉是辟公錫此祉也奔走在廟而貽我以
===
多福是辟公錫此福也然豈可輕忽遂訂哉蓋
惠我無窮使我子而又子永言保之也串錫無
疆使我孫而又孫勿替引之也厥功如此報之
當何如且爾在封邦也不封以專利不靡以傷
財著此愛民守法之盛德我固當隆其禮於今
日使之踰越等階以寵異之焉又念爾在宗廟
也盡誠以薦祉致孝以格□□□助祭錫福之
大功我又當致其報於後裔使之繼續封爵而
益大之焉然感發之意不盡故又戒勉之曰莫
punctuated:
考試官教授李，批：文體不類時作，則樣力過人遠矣，錄之爲經生式。

考試官教授濮，批：得工歌獻頌之體。

王者歸諸侯助祭之功，而示以報功之意，尤必戒勉之也。夫臣有功，君固當報之也，然又必有以戒勉之焉，其愛人以德之意何如哉！此祭於宗廟而獻助祭諸侯之樂歌，謂夫顧此烈文之辟公，相我宗廟之祀事。方其對越在天，而介我以繁祉，是辟公錫此祉也；奔走在廟，而貽我以多福，是辟公錫此福也。然豈可輕忽遂訂哉？蓋惠我無窮，使我子而又子，永言保之也；串錫無疆，使我孫而又孫，勿替引之也。厥功如此，報之當何如？且爾在封邦也，不封以專利，不靡以傷財，著此愛民守法之盛德。我固當隆其禮於今日，使之踰越等階，以寵異之焉。又念爾在宗廟也，盡誠以薦祉，致孝以格□□□助祭錫福之大功，我又當致其報於後裔，使之繼續封爵而益大之焉。然感發之意不盡，故又戒勉之曰：「莫
translation_en:
Examiner Li, Professor, comments: “The literary form differs from contemporary compositions, and its exemplary force [?] far surpasses that of others. It is recorded as a model for students of the Classics.”

Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: “It captures the form of a hymn sung by court musicians in offering praise.”

When a king attributes merit to the feudal lords for assisting at sacrifices and expresses his intention to reward that merit, he must above all admonish and encourage them. When a minister has rendered meritorious service, his ruler certainly ought to reward him; yet he must also find means to admonish and encourage him. How profound is his intention to cherish others through virtue! This is a ceremonial song performed at sacrifices in the ancestral temple and presented to the feudal lords who assist at them. It says: “Behold these lords, illustrious in achievement and cultured virtue, who assist in the sacrificial services of our ancestral temple. When they reverently respond to the spirits in Heaven and aid us with abundant blessings, it is these lords who bestow those blessings. When they hasten about the temple and bequeath us manifold good fortune, it is these lords who bestow that good fortune. How, then, could we treat this lightly and simply settle the matter [?]? They confer benefits upon us without end, enabling our sons and their sons to preserve them forever; they bestow blessings without limit [?], enabling our grandsons and their grandsons to continue them without interruption. Such being their merit, how should it be rewarded?

“Moreover, in your enfeoffed states, you do not aggrandize yourselves by monopolizing profits, nor squander resources through extravagance. You manifest the splendid virtue of loving the people and observing the laws. I should therefore accord you heightened ceremonial honors today, allowing you to rise above the usual grades of rank as a mark of special favor. I also consider how, in the ancestral temple, you offer blessings with utmost sincerity and exercise filial devotion to reach … [three illegible characters; connection uncertain] the great merit of assisting at sacrifices and bestowing blessings. I should also extend the reward to your descendants, allowing them to inherit your enfeoffed titles and enlarge them still further.”

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
強於人道以四方皆以為訓也莫顯於君德以
百辟皆以為刑也遂嗟嘆之以為我皇祖文王
沒矣其德所以彌久而人不能忘者無他術以
用此道焉我皇考武王往矣其德所以愈遠而
人不能忘者無餘法亦用此道焉爾辟公克盡
此道而備此德則所以報之者豈徒今日而已
哉吁既報之於前複戒之於後美不忘覲周之
王者真可謂得待諸侯之體者歟抑論諸侯之
致君得福此固臣之功也亦臣之分也周之王
===
者猶依然不忍忘褒其功德衍慶子孫且又以
道德之言而丁寧感發之蓋愛之無以尚報之
無以加真忠厚哉於戲山河帶礪之盟未衆而
家無噍類之禍旋及雖其臣之不能自全亦其
君之不能保全烈文之詩宜其萬世之永傳也
春秋
秋八月庚辰公及戎盟于唐〔隱公二年　春〕
王正月公如齊　夏仲孫蔑如京師
〔襄公九年〕
punctuated:
強於人道，以四方皆以為訓也；莫顯於君德，以百辟皆以為刑也。遂嗟嘆之，以為我皇祖文王沒矣，其德所以彌久而人不能忘者，無他術，以用此道焉。我皇考武王往矣，其德所以愈遠而人不能忘者，無餘法，亦用此道焉。爾辟公克盡此道而備此德，則所以報之者，豈徒今日而已哉？吁！既報之於前，複戒之於後，美不忘覲，周之王者真可謂得待諸侯之體者歟！抑論諸侯之致君得福，此固臣之功也，亦臣之分也。周之王者猶依然不忍忘，褒其功德，衍慶子孫，且又以道德之言而丁寧感發之。蓋愛之無以尚，報之無以加，真忠厚哉！於戲！山河帶礪之盟未衆，而家無噍類之禍旋及，雖其臣之不能自全，亦其君之不能保全。《烈文》之詩，宜其萬世之永傳也。

春秋
秋八月庚辰，公及戎盟于唐。〔隱公二年　春〕王正月，公如齊。夏，仲孫蔑如京師。〔襄公九年〕
translation_en:
… stronger than the way of human conduct, for all in the four quarters take it as their instruction; nothing is more manifest than a ruler’s virtue, for all the lords take it as their model. He then sighs in admiration, saying: “My august grandfather, King Wen, has died. That his virtue remains unforgettable as time passes is due to no other art than his practice of this way. My august father, King Wu, has departed. That his virtue remains unforgettable as his time grows more distant is due to no other method: he too practiced this way. If you, the lords, can fully realize this way and possess this virtue in its entirety, could your rewards possibly be confined to today?” Ah! Having first rewarded them, he subsequently admonished them again, praising them and not forgetting their attendance at court [?]. The king of Zhou may truly be said to have understood the proper manner of treating the feudal lords!

Yet, when we consider how the feudal lords enabled their ruler to receive blessings, this was indeed their achievement as subjects, but also their duty. Nevertheless, the king of Zhou still could not bear to forget them. He praised their achievements and virtue, extended blessings to their descendants, and further stirred and inspired them through earnest words about the Way and virtue. His love for them could not have been greater, nor could his recompense have been increased. How truly loyal and generous he was! Alas! Oaths pledging endurance until the rivers became like belts and the mountains like whetstones were not yet numerous [?], when calamity soon followed, leaving no living member of their households. Though this arose from the subjects’ inability to preserve themselves, it also arose from their rulers’ inability to protect them. The ode “Illustrious and Cultured” (Lie Wen) surely deserves to be transmitted forever through the ages.

Spring and Autumn Annals

In autumn, in the eighth month, on the gengchen day, the duke made a covenant with the Rong at Tang. 〔Second year of Duke Yin. Spring.〕 In the first month of the royal calendar, the duke went to Qi. In summer, Zhongsun Mie went to the royal capital. 〔Ninth year of Duke Xiang.〕

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
欸特書曰初稅畝之舉孰為之宣公因國用
之乏用增賦斂也聖人於此亦曰初者蓋謂井
田之制民得九公得一所以均上下古自殷人
而助周人而徹上惻怛以愛下下竭力以奉上
君民一體頌聲於作真可行之萬世矣傳至宣
公乃有稅畝之舉公私混於一途賦斂加於百
姓使先王分田制祿之良法於茲盡壞宣公不
可罪乎而後世效尤以自肆者則紛然繼起若成
公丘甲之作哀公田賦之用豈無自哉故特書
===
曰初吁樂有定制而魯僭之田有定法而魯廢
之安在其為秉禮哉抑因是而有感焉制禮樂
以教天下立井田以定人心者周公也周公欲
行之天下傳之萬世而身後與子孫皆違之九
原有知亦必有大不安者周公其衰矣乎孔子
安得而不嘆春秋安得而不作
禮記
求賜圭瓚則資鬯於天子天子命之教然
後為學
punctuated:
欸，特書曰「初」。稅畝之舉，孰為之？宣公因國用之乏，用增賦斂也。聖人於此亦曰「初」者，蓋謂井田之制，民得九，公得一，所以均上下。古自殷人而助，周人而徹，上惻怛以愛下，下竭力以奉上，君民一體，頌聲於作，真可行之萬世矣。傳至宣公，乃有稅畝之舉，公私混於一途，賦斂加於百姓，使先王分田制祿之良法於茲盡壞。宣公不可罪乎？而後世效尤以自肆者，則紛然繼起。若成公丘甲之作，哀公田賦之用，豈無自哉？故特書曰「初」。吁！樂有定制，而魯僭之；田有定法，而魯廢之。安在其為秉禮哉？抑因是而有感焉：制禮樂以教天下，立井田以定人心者，周公也。周公欲行之天下，傳之萬世，而身後與子孫皆違之。九原有知，亦必有大不安者。周公其衰矣乎？孔子安得而不嘆？春秋安得而不作？

禮記
求賜圭瓚，則資鬯於天子；天子命之教，然後為學。
translation_en:
…Ah [?], it specifically records the word “first.” Who instituted taxation by the mu? Duke Xuan, because state revenues were insufficient, used it to increase taxation. The Sage’s use of “first” here likewise means that under the well-field system the people received nine shares and the ruler one, thereby ensuring an equitable balance between those above and those below. In antiquity, from the Yin people’s system of communal assistance to the Zhou people’s system of shared assessment, those above compassionately cared for those below, and those below exerted themselves fully in serving those above. Ruler and people formed one body, and songs of praise arose [?]. Truly, this could have been practiced for ten thousand generations. Yet when it came down to Duke Xuan, taxation by the mu was instituted. Public and private lands were subjected to a single method of taxation, and additional levies were imposed upon the common people, utterly destroying the former kings’ sound arrangements for allocating land and establishing emoluments. Can Duke Xuan escape blame? In later generations, those who followed this bad example and gave themselves free rein arose in succession. Such measures as Duke Cheng’s imposition of military levies upon the qiu land units and Duke Ai’s levy upon farmland—could they have arisen without a source? Thus it specifically records “first.” Alas! Music had established regulations, yet Lu presumptuously overstepped them; land had established laws, yet Lu abolished them. Where, then, was its adherence to ritual? This also prompts a further reflection: it was the Duke of Zhou who established rites and music to instruct all under Heaven, and instituted the well-field system to settle the people’s hearts. The Duke of Zhou wished these institutions to be practiced throughout the realm and transmitted for ten thousand generations, yet after his death his descendants all violated them [?]. If he had awareness in the realm of the dead, he would surely be profoundly disquieted. Had the Duke of Zhou’s legacy fallen into such decline? How could Confucius refrain from lamenting? How could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to be written?

Record of Rites
When requesting the gift of a jade tablet and libation ladle, one obtains the aromatic sacrificial liquor from the Son of Heaven. Only after the Son of Heaven commands him to provide instruction does he establish a school.

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
王兕
同考試官教諭林　批　題本平易而難於
鋪叙此作詞整理足且以諸侯功德初受封
立說最是故錄之以為學禮者式
考試官教授李　批　禮教自天子出此作
得之
考試官教授濮　批　措詞平整
人臣備事神之禮也求於君人臣立教民之地
也聽於君蓋邑所以事神學所以教民也二者
===
皆不敢自專如此其一道德以尊天子也何如
哉記王制者知其然謂夫君之大柄不可以下
移臣之大分不可以上僭諸侯之行禮立教果
何如耶一惟請命於天子耳彼圭瓚者酌鬯之
爵而宗廟之祭未有重於鬯者也非瓚也天子
於諸侯必其功懋而後賜之功未懋者弗之賜
焉必其德盛然後錫之德未盛者弗之錫焉夫
然則鬯不敢以自為矣而宗廟之禮容可廢耶
於是春礿夏禘必請命於天子以求其鬯歸則
punctuated:
王兕

同考試官教諭林批：題本平易，而難於鋪叙。此作詞整、理足，且以諸侯功德、初受封立說，最是，故錄之以為學禮者式。

考試官教授李批：禮教自天子出，此作得之。

考試官教授濮批：措詞平整。

人臣備事神之禮也，求於君；人臣立教民之地也，聽於君。蓋邑所以事神，學所以教民也。二者皆不敢自專如此，其一道德以尊天子也何如哉！記《王制》者知其然，謂夫君之大柄不可以下移，臣之大分不可以上僭。諸侯之行禮立教，果何如耶？一惟請命於天子耳。彼圭瓚者，酌鬯之爵，而宗廟之祭未有重於鬯者也。非瓚也，天子於諸侯，必其功懋而後賜之，功未懋者弗之賜焉；必其德盛然後錫之，德未盛者弗之錫焉。夫然，則鬯不敢以自為矣，而宗廟之禮容可廢耶？於是春礿夏禘，必請命於天子以求其鬯，歸則
translation_en:
Wang Si

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: The topic is straightforward in itself, yet difficult to develop fully. This composition is orderly in expression and ample in reasoning. Particularly apt is its argument concerning the feudal lords’ merit and virtue and their initial enfeoffment. It has therefore been selected as a model for students of ritual.

Comment by Examiner Li, Professor: Ritual and instruction issue from the Son of Heaven. This composition grasps that point.

Comment by Examiner Pu, Professor: The wording is balanced and orderly.

When a subject prepares the rites for serving the spirits, he seeks what he needs from his ruler; when a subject establishes a place for instructing the people, he heeds his ruler. For the settlement [?] is that by which the spirits are served, and the school is that by which the people are instructed. In neither matter does he dare act on his own authority. How greatly this unifies moral principle and virtue, thereby honoring the Son of Heaven! The recorder of the “Royal Regulations” understood this: the ruler’s great authority must not pass downward, and the subject must not overstep his proper station and usurp what belongs above him. How, then, do the feudal lords perform rites and establish instruction? Solely by requesting authorization from the Son of Heaven.

The jade-handled libation ladle is a vessel for pouring aromatic sacrificial wine, and in sacrifices at the ancestral temple nothing is more important than this wine. “It is not the ladle” [?]. In his dealings with the feudal lords, the Son of Heaven bestows it only after their achievements have become outstanding; he does not bestow it upon those whose achievements are not yet outstanding. He grants it only after their virtue has become abundant; he does not grant it to those whose virtue is not yet abundant. This being so, they dare not make the aromatic wine on their own authority. Yet can the rites of the ancestral temple possibly be abandoned? Thus, for the yue sacrifice in spring and the di sacrifice in summer, they must request authorization from the Son of Heaven to obtain the aromatic wine. Upon returning, they then…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
圭璋瓚以是而灌地降神也秋嘗冬蒸必受
命於王朝以資其鬯歸則璋瓚是用以之而求
神於陰也人臣備事神之禮有求於君如此至
若教者化民之本而國家之一務未有重於學者
也是教也天子於諸侯既立國矣而民德當新
遂有泮汧之是頒焉既受封矣而民性當復斯
有綸音之是出焉夫然則學始得以自立矣而
一國之教其可緩耶於是經之營之建小學於
公宮南之左灑掃應對之儀於是乎肄習也規
===
之度之立大學於國門外之郊格致誠正之道
於是乎講明也人臣立教民之地有聽於君又
如此一卷之用一學之設皆有待於天子其尊
之也至矣大抵天下之勢不可以不一一則拳
有歸事有統世道愈隆矣故上文首曰天子賜
諸侯樂則以祝將之賜伯子男樂則以鼗將之
諸侯賜弓矢然後征賜鈇鉞然後殺於此又言
之若是合而觀之可見禮樂征伐教化皆出自
天子而諸侯不敢專也世道之隆何以如此孔
punctuated: 圭璋瓚以是而灌地降神也。秋嘗冬蒸，必受命於王朝，以資其鬯；歸則璋瓚是用，以之而求神於陰也。人臣備事神之禮，有求於君如此。至若教者，化民之本，而國家之一務未有重於學者也。是教也，天子於諸侯既立國矣，而民德當新，遂有泮汧之是頒焉；既受封矣，而民性當復，斯有綸音之是出焉。夫然則學始得以自立矣，而一國之教其可緩耶？於是經之營之，建小學於公宮南之左，灑掃應對之儀於是乎肄習也；規之度之，立大學於國門外之郊，格致誠正之道於是乎講明也。人臣立教民之地，有聽於君又如此。一卷之用，一學之設，皆有待於天子，其尊之也至矣。大抵天下之勢不可以不一，一則拳有歸，事有統，世道愈隆矣。故上文首曰：「天子賜諸侯樂，則以祝將之；賜伯子男樂，則以鼗將之。諸侯賜弓矢然後征，賜鈇鉞然後殺。」於此又言之若是，合而觀之，可見禮樂征伐、教化皆出自天子，而諸侯不敢專也。世道之隆何以如此？孔
translation_en:
…with libation ladles bearing gui and zhang jade handles, they pour this wine upon the ground to bring down the spirits. For the autumn chang and winter zheng sacrifices, they must receive authorization from the royal court to obtain their aromatic sacrificial wine. On returning, they use the zhang-handled libation ladle to seek the spirits in the yin realm below. Such is the dependence of ministers upon their ruler in preparing the rites for serving the spirits.

As for instruction, it is the foundation for transforming the people, and among the affairs of the state none is more important than schooling. In this matter of instruction, once the Son of Heaven has established states for the feudal lords, the people's virtue must be renewed; hence he grants them the pan and qian [?], the institutions of learning. Once they have received their enfeoffments, the people's original nature must be restored; hence royal pronouncements are issued. Only then may schools be established within their own domains. How, then, could the instruction of an entire state be delayed? Accordingly, they plan and build, establishing an elementary school to the left of the area south of the ducal palace. There the forms of sprinkling and sweeping, responding and answering are practiced. They lay out and measure, establishing a higher school in the outskirts beyond the city gates. There the Way of investigating things, extending knowledge, making intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind is expounded. Such, again, is the obedience ministers owe their ruler when establishing places for instructing the people.

The use of a single scroll [?] and the establishment of a single school both depend upon the Son of Heaven: the reverence accorded him is utmost. In general, authority throughout the world must be unified. When it is unified, power [?] has a locus and affairs have a governing order, and the moral order of the age flourishes all the more. Thus the preceding passage begins: “When the Son of Heaven grants music to feudal lords, he accompanies it with a zhu percussion instrument; when he grants music to earls, viscounts, and barons, he accompanies it with a pellet drum. Only after feudal lords have been granted bows and arrows may they undertake punitive expeditions; only after they have been granted axes of execution may they put people to death.” Here, too, it speaks in this manner. Taken together, these statements show that ritual, music, punitive expeditions, and moral instruction all proceed from the Son of Heaven, and that the feudal lords dare not exercise independent authority over them. How does the moral order of the age attain such flourishing? Confucius…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
孔子曰天下有道則禮樂征伐自天子出
事君大言入則望大利
吳儀

===
下之事上也既納非常之論則期非常之功盖
言之大者功必大也人臣非常之論既見納於
上矣得不以非常之功而自期哉見於表記其
旨如此謂天人臣之事君也以下奉上以卑承
尊所知宜無不諫所見宜無不告是故一獻納
也莫非嘉謀嘉猷有以致君之從一論思也無
非弘規遠圖有以動君之聽道莫大乎仁義而
仁義在所當言也必以仁義之大言日陳於前
臣曰是帝亦曰是無咈逆焉政莫大乎教養而
punctuated:
孔子曰：「天下有道，則禮樂征伐自天子出。」

事君，大言入，則望大利。
吳儀

下之事上也，既納非常之論，則期非常之功。盖言之大者，功必大也。人臣非常之論既見納於上矣，得不以非常之功而自期哉？見於表記，其旨如此。謂天人臣之事君也，以下奉上，以卑承尊，所知宜無不諫，所見宜無不告。是故一獻納也，莫非嘉謀嘉猷，有以致君之從；一論思也，無非弘規遠圖，有以動君之聽。道莫大乎仁義，而仁義在所當言也，必以仁義之大言日陳於前，臣曰是，帝亦曰是，無咈逆焉。政莫大乎教養，而
translation_en:
Confucius said: “When the Way prevails throughout the realm, rites, music, and punitive expeditions issue from the Son of Heaven.”

“In serving one's ruler, when momentous counsel is accepted, one expects momentous benefits.”
Wu Yi
Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: “This topic already has a clear commentary; a straightforward exposition is all that is needed. Many candidates interpreted it through the preceding passage about serving others, which seems rather forced. This essay alone bases its composition on the transmitted commentary and captures the meaning.”
Examiner Li, Professor, comments: “The language flows smoothly, and the reasoning is clear.”
Examiner Pu, Professor, comments: “The exposition of momentous counsel and momentous benefits is very clear. Might the author himself aspire to offer momentous counsel?”

When a subordinate serves his superior, once extraordinary counsel has been accepted, he expects extraordinary accomplishments. For counsel of great import must yield great accomplishments. Once a minister's extraordinary counsel has been accepted by his ruler, can he fail to set extraordinary accomplishments as his own goal? Such is the meaning of the passage in the Record of Exemplary Conduct (Biaoji). That is to say [?], when a minister serves his ruler, he attends upon his superior from below and supports the exalted from a lowly position. Whatever he knows, he should offer in remonstrance; whatever he sees, he should report. Thus every presentation of counsel consists of excellent plans and sound proposals capable of securing the ruler's assent; every deliberation consists of broad designs and far-reaching plans capable of gaining the ruler's attention. Nothing in the Way is greater than benevolence and righteousness. Since benevolence and righteousness are matters on which he ought to speak, he must daily present momentous counsel concerning them before the ruler. The minister says, “This is right,” and the emperor likewise says, “This is right,” with no opposition between them. Nothing in government is greater than educating and nourishing the people, and…

title: 弘治十一年河南鄉試錄
text:
教養在所當言也必以教養之大言日進於上
臣曰可君亦曰可無扞格焉夫大言既入則諫
行言聽而吾道可大行矣足以心之所期惟欲
所獻納者措諸政事之間以臻其時驗志之所
願惟冀所論思者見諸設施之際以著其極功
如仁義之言陳矣則望吾君以仁而育萬民以
義而正萬民使仁義之澤遍敷九有而流惠無
窮天下後世同一利也如教養之言進矣則望
吾君以教而復民性以養而厚民生使教養之
===
澤覃被四海而垂裕無巳天下後世均一利也
吁因其言之所入而望其功之所成如此人臣
事君之忠也何如哉抑考古之為臣者其經世
之學皆預定於巳至於事君則前定之規模先
形於言以為籍然後自獻其身以成其信也苟
言焉未入而欲望其利之及人得乎嗚呼大言
入則望大利小言入則望小利臣之所以事其
君者固如此而君之所以報其臣者何如亦必
視其言之大小而養之以祿耳故曰不以小言
punctuated:
教養在所當言也，必以教養之大言日進於上。臣曰可，君亦曰可，無扞格焉。夫大言既入，則諫行言聽，而吾道可大行矣。足以心之所期，惟欲所獻納者措諸政事之間，以臻其時驗；志之所願，惟冀所論思者見諸設施之際，以著其極功。如仁義之言陳矣，則望吾君以仁而育萬民，以義而正萬民，使仁義之澤遍敷九有，而流惠無窮，天下後世同一利也。如教養之言進矣，則望吾君以教而復民性，以養而厚民生，使教養之澤覃被四海，而垂裕無巳，天下後世均一利也。
吁！因其言之所入，而望其功之所成如此，人臣事君之忠也何如哉！抑考古之為臣者，其經世之學皆預定於巳。至於事君，則前定之規模先形於言，以為籍，然後自獻其身，以成其信也。苟言焉未入，而欲望其利之及人，得乎？嗚呼！大言入，則望大利；小言入，則望小利。臣之所以事其君者固如此，而君之所以報其臣者何如？亦必視其言之大小，而養之以祿耳。故曰：「不以小言
translation_en:
…Education and sustenance are matters on which one ought to speak, and one must therefore daily submit weighty proposals concerning them to the sovereign. When the minister says, “This is acceptable,” the ruler likewise says, “This is acceptable,” with no opposition or obstruction. Once weighty proposals have been accepted, remonstrances are acted upon and counsel heeded, and our Way can be put broadly into practice. As for what the heart anticipates [?], one desires only that the counsel submitted be applied in government affairs and achieve practical results in its time [?]; as for what the will aspires to, one hopes only that the deliberations offered be embodied in measures undertaken and manifest their fullest achievement. Thus, once proposals concerning benevolence and righteousness have been presented, one looks to our ruler to nurture all the people through benevolence and set them right through righteousness, so that their blessings spread throughout the nine regions and confer benefits without end, benefiting equally all under Heaven and generations to come. Once proposals concerning education and sustenance have been submitted, one looks to our ruler to restore the people’s moral nature through education and enrich their livelihoods through sustenance, so that these blessings extend throughout the Four Seas and bequeath prosperity without cease, benefiting equally all under Heaven and generations to come.
Ah! To look for accomplishments commensurate with the counsel accepted in this way—how great is a minister’s loyalty in serving his ruler! Moreover, if we examine those who served as ministers in antiquity, their learning concerning the governance of the world was already firmly established within themselves. When they came to serve their rulers, the plans already settled upon first took shape in words as a pledge; they then devoted themselves personally to fulfilling that pledge. If one’s counsel has not yet been accepted, can one hope that its benefits will reach others? Alas! When weighty proposals are accepted, one looks for great benefits; when lesser proposals are accepted, one looks for lesser benefits. Such, indeed, is how a minister serves his ruler. And how should the ruler recompense his minister? He too must assess the importance of the minister’s proposals and support him with an appropriate stipend. Thus it is said: “Do not, for lesser proposals …
